text: Labeling everything once is the easy part. The hard part is keeping those labels accurate as new data gets created daily and the people who applied the original labels move on. This lesson covers the governance program that keeps a classification scheme meaningful after the initial rollout.

Four roles split the work. The data owner, usually business-side, is accountable for a dataset and decides what classification it should carry. The data steward actually applies that classification in practice, tagging it in the catalog and keeping it current. The data custodian, usually IT, implements the controls a classification level requires, the encryption, the access restriction, the logging. And the governance committee owns the scheme itself, the tier definitions, and how disputes get resolved.

Classification drift is what happens when a dataset's actual sensitivity and its applied label quietly stop matching. A table that started as aggregate statistics gets a new column with individual-level data, and nobody revisits its Internal label. A dataset that was genuinely Confidential becomes effectively public once the same numbers appear in an earnings report, and the label never gets downgraded. None of that is a failure of the scheme itself, it's a failure of governance, nothing forced anyone to check.

The fix is a scheduled, recurring review, not a one-time audit. Restricted-tier data gets reviewed most frequently, for example quarterly. Public-tier data gets reviewed least frequently, annually or not at all, since there's little harm in an outdated public label. Each review asks whether the structure changed, whether the original justification still holds, and whether anything new entered the dataset.

That closes the full lifecycle of a label: the scheme, finding the data, applying it, and keeping it accurate. None of it matters if nothing downstream reads the label. Next up: access governance, the first of several controls that turn a classification label into an actual access decision.
